<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-supported cases, but B sustained more threads through the full exchange while A's case narrowed. A's strongest move was exposing that CON's preferred alternative (income-driven repayment) is itself a taxpayer-funded permanent write-off, reframing CON's "pricing" as gratuitous suffering — a genuinely damaging point that B never fully rebutted head-on except by drawing a timing distinction (IDR keeps monitoring and can recapture rising income; discharge severs that link permanently). That distinction, especially crystallized in "the credential waits patiently," was B's most effective and original contribution, and it survived to the end largely unanswered in A's closing, which pivoted entirely to the suffering-as-pricing frame. Meanwhile B's access/adverse-selection argument (tighter lending hurting marginal, first-gen borrowers) was pressed in rebuttal 1 and reinforced in rebuttal 2, but A dropped this thread entirely after an initial reply, leaving it live for B. A's case also suffered two word-limit clippings, a real execution cost that cut off developing arguments. B's speeches were consistently complete, tightly organized, and directly responsive, including clean A1/A2 compliance after pressure questions. On balance, B did more to neutralize A's core claims than A did to neutralize B's, giving B a clear but not overwhelming edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's distinction in Rebuttal 2 (B4.1–B4.3) between IDR's ongoing, income-sensitive recapture versus bankruptcy's one-time, irreversible discharge — crystallized as "the credential waits patiently, revives the day after the debt dies" — was the most decisive exchange, since A's closing never fully rebutted the asymmetry beyond reasserting that eligibility requires sustained past inability, which doesn't address post-discharge income recovery.</best_rebuttal>
